props.title: Big Fan

sections.content: Big Fan stands as one of cinema's most unflinching looks at sports obsession, with Patton Oswalt delivering a devastating performance as Paul Aufiero, a parking garage attendant whose entire identity revolves around the New York Giants. The film shares DNA with The King of Comedy (1982) and Taxi Driver (1976) in its examination of lonely men on society's margins, but writer-director Robert Siegel (who wrote The Wrestler (2008)) takes a more grounded approach. Unlike those Scorsese classics, there's no glamorization of violence or delusion here - just the raw reality of fandom as religion.

sections.content: What makes Big Fan particularly effective is how it captures the tribal nature of sports fandom. Paul's late-night calls to sports radio become his pulpit, his parking booth a confessional where he crafts elaborate defenses of his beloved team. The film shares thematic territory with Silver Linings Playbook (2012) in exploring how sports loyalty can both unite and isolate, though Big Fan takes a much darker path. When Paul's idol, Giants linebacker Quantrell Bishop, brutally attacks him at a strip club, the film becomes a disturbing study of denial and misplaced devotion.

Siegel's direction maintains an uncomfortable intimacy, forcing us to live in Paul's confined world - his childhood bedroom in his mother's house, his tiny parking booth, the glow of sports radio at 2 AM. It's reminiscent of the claustrophobic character studies of Foxcatcher (2014) and Nightcrawler (2014), where obsession warps into something dangerous. The film's power comes from its refusal to judge Paul while still showing the tragic consequences of his unwavering fandom. SUBHEAD: The Dark Side of Fandom

sections.content: While many sports films celebrate the communal joy of fandom, Big Fan belongs to a darker subset that explores its pathological extremes, alongside films like The Fan (1996) and Celtic Pride (1996). Paul's rivalry with Philadelphia Eagles superfan Philadelphia Phil mirrors real-world sports rivalries that sometimes turn violent. The film predates but perfectly captures today's toxic fan culture, where identity becomes so wrapped up in teams that rational thought disappears.
